steps.say: Most diaphragmatic hernias come through the posterolateral Bochdalek defect, usually on the left. Bowel in the chest pushes the mediastinum across, and a feeding tube coiling upward confirms the stomach has herniated.
steps.tx: **Bochdalek hernia anatomy** places the defect posterolaterally, forming **85-90%** of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and occurring on the **left side in 80-85%**. Bowel loops fill the hemithorax, the mediastinum shifts away, the abdomen looks scaphoid, and a nasogastric tube tip coiling in the chest confirms herniated stomach.

steps.say: The Morgagni hernia is hidden behind the sternum, usually on the right, and often contains liver or omentum. Because symptoms stay mild, a lateral film taken for something else frequently reveals it.
steps.tx: **Morgagni hernia location** is retrosternal and anterior, forming only **5-10%** of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and appearing mostly on the right. Herniated liver or omentum sits behind the sternum, respiratory morbidity stays low, and many lesions surface incidentally on a lateral chest film taken for another reason.

steps.say: Congenital pulmonary airway malformations are hamartomatous lung tissue connected to the normal tracheobronchial tree. The Stocker classification is based on cyst size, from large macrocysts to microscopic solid architecture.
steps.tx: **CPAM Stocker classification** categorizes congenital pulmonary airway malformations based on cyst diameter. **Type I macrocystic** malformations feature single or multiple large cysts exceeding **2 cm** with thin walls; Type II lesions feature uniform cysts under 2 cm; and Type III lesions are microcystic solid-appearing adenomatoid masses. Type 1 cysts measure **2-10 cm**, Type 2 cysts stay **under 2 cm**, and Type 3 lesions look solid.

rows: Uniform small cysts, frequent renal anomalies

steps.say: Extralobar sequestration wraps itself in its own pleura and drains to systemic veins in most cases. Its aortic feeder and frequent partner anomalies separate it clearly from the intralobar type.
steps.tx: **Extralobar sequestration features** start with a separate visceral pleural envelope around non-functioning lung tissue. Systemic arterial supply rises from the aorta, systemic venous drainage reaches the azygos system in about **80%**, and associated diaphragmatic or cardiac anomalies are commoner than in the intralobar form.

steps.say: Intralobar sequestration lives inside normal lung pleura and drains back through the pulmonary veins. Recurrent infection in the same basal segment during later childhood usually brings it to attention.
steps.tx: **Intralobar sequestration features** describe dysplastic lung sharing the visceral pleura of normal adjacent lung. A systemic aortic feeder still supplies the segment, yet drainage returns through normal pulmonary veins in about **95%**, and recurrent basal pneumonia in an older child is the usual presentation.

steps.say: A bronchogenic cyst is typically located under the carina as a smooth round middle mediastinal mass. It never connects to the airway, although a large one can squeeze the carina in a small infant.
steps.tx: **Bronchogenic cyst location** is usually subcarinal or elsewhere in the middle mediastinum, where these foregut duplication cysts sit as smooth, well-marginated round masses. They never communicate with the airway, stay soft-tissue or fluid density on CT (computed tomography), and can compress the carina in infants.

steps.say: Weak bronchial cartilage lets air in but traps it on expiration, so one lobe overinflates. The left upper and middle lobes dominate, and the swollen lobe steadily compresses the healthier lung.
steps.tx: **Congenital lobar emphysema** follows bronchial cartilage hypoplasia (underdevelopment) causing ball-valve hyperinflation of one lobe. The **left upper lobe takes 42%**, the **middle lobe 35%** and the right upper lobe most of the remainder, with progressive air trapping, mediastinal shift and compression of the surviving lung.

steps.say: A cystic lung lesion in a young child is never dismissed as a simple malformation. DICER1 related pleuropulmonary blastoma can look identical to a benign cyst, which is why excision matters.
steps.tx: **Pleuropulmonary blastoma risk** changes how every cystic lung lesion is read, because **DICER1 gene mutations** predispose to Type 1 cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma. It mimics Type 1 CPAM (congenital pulmonary airway malformation) on imaging, so resection and histology, not observation alone, settle the diagnosis safely.
